The Torah Teaching, Philosophical System and Public Work of the Maharal of Prague
This text offers a comprehensive and in-depth survey of the figure of the Maharal of Prague, sketching the outlines of his philosophical system, his public work and his influence over the generations. The author presents the Maharal not only as a halakhic authority but as a thinker who created an orderly metaphysical system based on the relations of matter and form, the "straight line" versus the "circle," and the symbolic meaning of numbers. The body of the text analyzes the Maharal's conception of redemption as a cosmic necessity deriving from the "law of the natural place," alongside a survey of his central works, which defend the tradition of the Sages and promote a pedagogical reform based on gradualism and rectitude of thought. Finally, the source distinguishes between the popular myth of the Golem and the historical reality, and concludes by describing the vitality of his thought in modern currents such as Hasidism and Religious Zionism.
The Torah Teaching, Philosophical System and Public Work of the Maharal of Prague
Introduction: The Historical Background and Public Leadership
Rabbi Yehuda Liva ben Bezalel, known in rabbinic literature as a halakhic and intellectual authority by the appellation Maharal (Our Teacher the Great, Rabbi Liva) of Prague, and in German literature by the title "Rabbi Loew the High," was active in the late sixteenth century and the early seventeenth century, a period that marks the transition of the Torah world from the age of the Rishonim to the beginning of the Acharonim period.[1] The Maharal, who lived approximately between the years 5272–5369 (1512/1520–1609), was a halakhic decisor, a Kabbalist of great stature and an exceptional religious thinker, whose written and rhetorical teaching continued to radiate and influence across many generations in all the Jewish communities of the Diaspora.[1, 2]
The Maharal's work went beyond the sphere of purely intellectual creativity; he led his community in Prague with a strong hand and maintained a close and respectful relationship with the imperial authorities.[2] A central testimony to the Maharal's public standing is the historic meeting between him and the Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, Rudolf II, who sent an official emissary to invite him to the royal court.[3] The meeting between the two was marked by a warm reception and a personal face-to-face conversation, whose exact content remained sealed and closed in the annals of history.[3] These close relations with the monarchy contributed greatly to the security and welfare of the Jews of Prague at that time, and the Maharal even maintained indirect ties with the famous court astronomer Tycho Brahe through his student, the historian and scientist Rabbi David Gans.[2, 3] His figure left such a tremendous impression on the city of Prague that in later times an official statue was erected in his memory in the Czech capital—a unique case in which a foreign capital city saw fit to commemorate a Jewish rabbi with a public monument.[4]
The Maharal's student, Rabbi David Gans, described his teacher as "the crown of the sages and exemplar of our generations, by whose light all nations will walk."[4] This description reflects the immense esteem that the Maharal enjoyed even in his lifetime, an esteem that stemmed from his methodical ability to create a comprehensive philosophical system that endows all levels of the Torah with deep spiritual meaning.[2] The Maharal developed an entire and organized literary canon intended to clarify the foundations of religion and Jewish existence.[2] Below is a table presenting the Maharal's central works and the metaphysical and cosmological aims that they serve in the overall system of thought.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Metaphysical Structure: Matter, Form and the Spatial Geometry of Numbers
At the center of the Maharal's philosophical system stands an original use of the pair of metaphysical concepts "matter" and "form," which originate in Aristotelian philosophy, but he endows them with a distinct Kabbalistic and theological tint.[14] According to the Maharal's definition, any entity that serves as the soul and source of vitality for another entity is called "form," while the substrate that bears it and enables its expression is called "matter."[14] In the hierarchical structure of the cosmos, the people of Israel function as "form" in relation to the physical world, which serves them as "matter."[14] The Torah, for its part, is the "form" of Israel, while the Holy One, blessed be He, is the "ultimate and absolute form" of all of reality.[14] This relation of matter and form is also reflected in the institutions of physical life, such as the pairing of man and woman, which constitutes a wholeness of material and formal fusion that receives its existence from the name of the Creator.[14]
This distinction between the limited material dimension and the metaphysical spiritual dimension is formulated by the Maharal by means of a geometric image of "the circle" versus "the straight line."[13] The natural sciences, which describe the mechanical and cyclical order of the universe, are represented by the circle (which reflects the medieval conception of the celestial bodies and spheres; hence the Hebrew word "siba," "cause," which denotes revolution, "sibuv," and fixed causality).[13] This circular order is deterministic and leaves no room for free choice or moral demand.[13] By contrast, the Torah is represented by "the straight line"—a line that leads directly from the source to the human being and defines the space of choice and moral preference.[13] The human being is distinguished from all creatures in that he was created in a state of potential only ("in power"), and his purpose in life is to bring his perfection into actuality ("in act") through the observance of the Torah and the commandments.[8] The soul, whose source is in heaven, stands in the lower and imperfect world, and the Torah was given to it in order to complete its essential lack.[8] All of reality strives incessantly toward a primary perfection called "completion to one," which is revealed gradually across time and space.[13]
In order to explain the ways of divine governance within the natural and supernatural space, the Maharal developed a systematic "doctrine of numbers" and geometric space.[9, 13] The Maharal distinguished in principle between odd numbers, which express joining, convergence and wholeness, and even numbers, which represent multiplicity, division and opposing sides.[9] Below is a table detailing the metaphysical meaning of the numbers in the Maharal's system.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Historiosophy of Exile and Redemption: The Law of the Natural Place and the Linguistic Analysis
In his monumental historiosophical work "Netzach Yisrael" ("The Eternity of Israel"), composed of 63 chapters, the Maharal sets out a broad and innovative theological doctrine dealing with the laws of Jewish history.[11, 16] He opens with the assertion that in order to attain true knowledge of redemption, one must first clarify the matter of exile and destruction, since all things are acquired through their opposites—like the black color from which the white color is discerned and measured.[12] This principle underlies the determination of the Talmudic sages to begin the telling of the Passover Haggadah with "disgrace" and to conclude with "praise," because there is no true recognition of praise except through its opposite.[12]
The Maharal formulates an unchanging physical-metaphysical law: everything in creation has a "natural place" that is fitting for it.[12] The natural place of fire is above, whereas the natural place of earth is below.[12] If a person forces part of the fire to remain below or part of the earth to remain above, this situation will remain unnatural and temporary, for it is impossible that the unnatural should become permanently natural forever.[12] This law is applied directly to the national existence of the people of Israel:
Alteration of the natural order: The Holy One, blessed be He, arranged every nation in its fitting place, and the natural place of Israel is in the Land of Israel.[12] Exile is a complete departure from the natural order.[12]
The law of the gathering of the dispersion: National dispersion contradicts the laws of nature.[12] All the parts of a single entity strive to unite and return to their place.[12] Since the people of Israel is one undivided nation, their dispersion among the nations is an extremely unnatural state.[12]
The metaphysical necessity of redemption: Since an unnatural state cannot become natural and endure forever, the very existence of exile constitutes a clear and irrefutable metaphysical proof of the necessary coming of the future redemption.[12]
This understanding is sharpened by means of a comparative linguistic analysis of the verbs "galah" (to go into exile) and "ga'al" (to redeem), which share the same base letters (gimel and lamed).[13] The difference lies in the final letter: the word "galah" ends with the letter heh, which is formally composed of the letter dalet and a dot, symbolizing the dispersion to the four directions of heaven.[13] By contrast, in the word "ga'al" the letter aleph appears in the middle of the word, symbolizing the "Master of the World" (aluf shel olam), who gathers the dispersion and unites it at the center.[13] From this it emerges that exile itself is the cause of redemption, since it preserves the potential for Israel's unity precisely from within the dispersion.[13] Below is a table detailing the thematic and textual structure of the book "Netzach Yisrael" according to its various chapters, demonstrating how these processes are built into his system.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Talmudic Apologetics and Freedom of Expression in "Be'er HaGolah"
The book "Be'er HaGolah" ("The Well of the Exile"), written approximately between the years 5335–5355 (1575–1595) and first printed in the year 5358 (1598), is a comprehensive defensive work on the standing of the Oral Torah and the authority of the Talmudic sages.[6, 7, 17] The work was written as a direct continuation of "Tiferet Yisrael" ("The Glory of Israel") and, unlike the Maharal's other books, makes distinctive use of rhymed writing in certain sections.[6, 7] The Maharal divided the work into seven gates called "wells," through which he rejects seven central claims that were directed against the Sages in his time [6, 7]:
The First Well ("Holy Waters"): Responds to the claim that the Sages added commandments (such as the washing of hands and the eruv tavshilin) or subtracted from them (such as limiting the lashes to 39 instead of 40) contrary to the biblical prohibition "You shall not add and you shall not subtract."[6, 7]
The Second Well ("Pure Waters"): Deals with the claim that the Sages' enactments were established contrary to sound reasoning and human intellect.[6, 7]
The Third Well ("Sweet Waters"): Answers the criticism that the Sages interpreted the verses contrary to the literal meaning and to the rules of grammar and pronunciation.[6, 7]
The Fourth Well ("Living Waters"): Clarifies the aggadic midrashim that attribute human traits to God, such as weeping, prayer or the putting on of tefillin.[6, 7]
The Fifth Well ("Deep Waters"): Rejects claims that the Talmud contains illogical or immodest tall tales.[6, 7]
The Sixth Well ("Mighty Waters"): Answers the claim that the words of the Sages on matters of science, medicine and astronomy are not correct.[6, 7]
The Seventh Well ("Pure Waters"): Defends the legal integrity of the Sages against accusations of vengefulness or discrimination toward non-Jews.[6, 7]
At the conclusion of the Sixth Well, the Maharal turns to a sharp and inexplicable criticism of the views of Rabbi Azariah de' Rossi in his book "Me'or Einayim" ("Light of the Eyes").[7] The Maharal completely rejected de' Rossi's attempt to evaluate the words of the Sages with external historical and scientific tools.[7] According to the Maharal, the words of the Sages do not deal with the physical-material layer of nature but with the supreme spiritual causes and the metaphysical order, and therefore subjecting them to the test of human scientific tools is a category error.[7, 13]
Alongside his intellectual conservatism and his defense of the Sages, in "Be'er HaGolah" the Maharal formulated a principled and innovative defense of freedom of expression and open debate.[14] He protested forcefully against the religious censorship of his time, and determined, in universal formulations, that force must not be used to remove or silence opinions opposed to faith and religion.[14] The Maharal compared religious debate to a battle, and argued that a victor can take pride in his victory only if his opponent was given the full opportunity to wage a free and fair struggle.[14] The silencing of opposing opinions creates an impression of weakness and prevents the truth from being clarified in its full glory.[14]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Pedagogical Reform and the Opposition to Pilpul
The Maharal's sharpest criticism at the communal level was directed at the Jewish educational system in Ashkenaz and Poland.[4] The Maharal lashed out against the deviation from studying the Talmud according to its plain meaning, and condemned the teachers and the parents for the stagnation in instruction and the shift to study based on "crooked paths of pilpulim, distinctions and empty sharpenings."[4] He argued that this method damages the student's sound judgment and produces mechanical study without true understanding, in which "the child will chirp words aloud, and the picture of the plain meaning he will not know."[4]
Against the existing state of affairs, the Maharal proposed a comprehensive reform based on the following stages [4]:
Gradualism of study: Strict implementation of the sequence of ages established in the Mishnah—at five for Scripture, at ten for Mishnah, and at fifteen for Gemara.[4] He opposed with all his might the sudden leap from the Chumash directly to the study of Gemara.[4]
Orderly study of Scripture: A demand to study the five books of the Torah in their full order and not in disconnected excerpts, with absolute focus on the plain meaning of the text, and the establishment of an obligation to study also the books of the Prophets and the Writings—subjects that were completely neglected in Ashkenaz at that time.[4]
Establishing the study of Mishnah: Orderly study of mishnayot, giving priority to tractates whose subjects are practiced in our generation, and only afterward moving on to the tractates of Kodashim and Tohorot.[4] The Maharal raged at the neglect of the Mishnah, which was the greatest educational deficiency of his time.[4]
Acquiring practical halakha: Study of daily halakha from the Gemara, and teaching the Shulchan Arukh to students in advance of the festivals and holidays so that they will be well versed in the practical laws.[4]
The Maharal established the concept of "rectitude" (yosher) as a guiding motif in study.[13] For this reason he recommended that the young student avoid, at the first stage, studying the commentary of the Tosafot, and focus on studying the plain meaning with Rashi's commentary, which offers a basic and straightforward explanation.[13] Only when the student's judgment is established and stable may he ascend to levels of pilpul and complex analysis.[13] This approach stood in complete contrast to the education accepted at that time, in which already at the age of nine the child was required to study a page of Gemara with Tosafot independently.[4]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Golem of Prague: From Kabbalistic Clay Figures to the Attic of the Altneuschul Synagogue
In the public and popular consciousness, the figure of the Maharal is identified with the story of the creation of "the Golem of Prague."[13, 18, 19] The term "golem" is used by the Sages to describe primary raw material (such as a lump of clay or a block of wood) that requires processing, and also to describe a simple and coarse person whose intellect and emotions have not yet developed.[20] The myth relates that the Maharal, in order to protect his community from blood libels and antisemitic pogroms in the Jewish Quarter of Prague (Josefov), created a giant figure from earth and breathed life into it by engraving the word "emet" ("truth") on its forehead.[19, 21] The Golem obeyed his commands, but when the Maharal forgot to deactivate it on Sabbath eve, the Golem desecrated the Sabbath and went out of control.[19, 21] The Maharal located it near the ancient synagogue "Altneuschul," erased the letter aleph from its forehead and left the word "met" ("dead").[19, 21] The remains of the Golem's clay body were placed, according to the legend, in the attic of the synagogue, and entry there was forbidden for hundreds of years.[19, 21]
From the standpoint of thought, the ability to create a human-like being rests on the words of the Amora Rava in the Talmud: "If the righteous wished, they could create a world."[20] The righteous, who are clean of any sin that separates them from God, are capable of using the metaphysical powers embedded in the letters of the Holy Tongue and in the combinations of names that appear in the "Sefer Yetzirah" ("Book of Formation") in order to bring forth a physical reality.[20]
However, the study of literature and history reveals an absolute gap between the historical myth and reality [18, 19]:
Absence of historical documentation: There is no mention of the Golem in the writings of the Maharal, in the writings of his students, or in Jewish and Christian sources from the 16th and 17th centuries.[4, 19]
Modern pseudepigraphy: The main source of the story in its familiar version is the book "The Golem of Prague and Other Wondrous Deeds," written by Rabbi Yehuda Yudel Rosenberg in the early twentieth century.[18, 19] Rosenberg presented the book as a translation of an ancient manuscript, but scholars such as Eli Yassif have proven that it is a literary forgery and a complete fabrication.[18, 19] On the other hand, other scholars attempted to search for findings in the attic of the Altneuschul in order to find a historical kernel to the story.[19]
Tremendous cultural influence: Despite being a late fabrication, the Golem became one of the most influential myths in Western culture.[18, 19] It gave the world the common expression "the Golem rose up against its creator" and served as a source of inspiration for Paul Wegener's silent film of 1920, for the book of Isaac Bashevis Singer, and also for characters in modern media such as Captain America, Shtisel and more.[19, 22]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Reception of His Thought and Its Development in the Modern Era
Although the Maharal's educational reforms were not accepted immediately in his generation, his metaphysical and philosophical thought became one of the pillars of major spiritual movements in the modern era.[1, 13, 23] Below is a table summarizing the central axes of influence of the Maharal's teaching on Jewish currents of thought and education over the generations.
The literary enterprise of Rabbi Yehoshua Hartman symbolizes the modern peak of the reception of the Maharal's teaching.[23] The edition includes extensive introductions, detailed footnotes that compare the Maharal's words in various places, and structured links to the writings of Rabbi Yitzchak Hutner.[23] At the same time, there exists a constant tension in the world of learners between the thick scholarly editions and the need of the average student for more "lean" and popular editions.[23]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
The thought of the Maharal of Prague constitutes an intellectual cathedral that unites, in an unprecedented manner, the revealed world and the hidden world, and rigid philosophical principles with vital biblical homiletics.[2, 13] Through the geometric concepts of "the straight line" and "the circle," and a metaphysical analysis of the concept of "the natural place," the Maharal succeeded in giving cosmic meaning to the tragedy of exile and in establishing the eternity and necessity of national redemption.[12, 13] His philosophical defense of the Oral Torah in his work "Be'er HaGolah," alongside the rejection of the reductionist-historical approach, is surprisingly accompanied by the formulation of an early manifesto for freedom of expression and fair debate.[7, 14] His demand for an educational reform adapted to the natural development of the child, and for integrating Scripture and Mishnah as the basis for Talmud, positions him as an original pedagogue ahead of his time.[4] Even if his figure was adorned over the generations with the clay-animating legends of the Golem, his actual spiritual legacy continues to be a source of vitality, inspiration and guidance across the generations in the world of Hasidism, in Religious Zionism and in the halls of the yeshivot in the modern era.[1, 13, 29]
